result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Building a Risk Prediction Model" subtitle: "Prediction vs explanation · outcome and predictors · events per variable · predicted risks · risk groups · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Earlier workshops: **explain** (the effect of an exposure) - Today: **predict** (the **risk for one patient**), as in a **screening score** - By the end you can: - state the **aim** of a prediction model and the main **steps** (TRIPOD) - check the **sample size** (events per variable) - fit a model and give a **predicted risk** and **risk groups** ::: ## Prediction is not explanation | | Explanation | Prediction | |---|---|---| | Aim | an **unbiased effect** of one exposure | **accurate risks** for new patients | | Variables | chosen by **causal reasoning** (confounders) | chosen for **predictive value**, available at the time of use | | Judged by | bias, CI of the effect | **discrimination, calibration**, usefulness | | Risk | confounding | **overfitting**, poor transport | ::: {.key} Coefficients of correlated predictors need **not** be interpretable in a prediction model; what matters is **how well the predicted risks work in new patients**. ::: ## Our problem: screening for undiagnosed diabetes ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **Development cohort**: **700 adults** from one district, **84 (12%)** with undiagnosed diabetes - 8 candidate predictors: age, sex, BMI, waist, family history, hypertension, activity, smoking - 10 extra lab markers (m1 to m10) used in Session 3 - **Validation cohort**: **2,000 adults** from **another district** (Session 5) - Aim: a **risk score** to decide who gets a **blood test** ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dev |> select(age, sex, bmi, waist, fam_history, hypertension, activity, smoker, diabetes) |> head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 9 age sex bmi waist fam_history hypertension activity smoker diabetes 1 29 Female 19.6 69 1 0 1.4 0 0 2 68 Male 22.9 84 0 1 1.1 0 0 3 33 Female 28.3 104 0 0 8.4 0 0 4 37 Male 31.5 116 1 0 4.5 1 0 5 31 Male 22.5 86 0 0 0.3 0 0 6 33 Female 26 91 1 0 4.1 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — Is the sample big enough? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Events per variable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(adults = nrow(dev), events = sum(dev$diabetes), prevalence = mean(dev$diabetes)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` adults events prevalence 700.00 84.00 0.12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(dev$diabetes) / 8 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} It is the **number of events** (the rarer outcome), not the number of adults, that limits the model. **84 events for 8 parameters** = **10.5 events per parameter**, just at the **rule of thumb (10)**. Newer criteria (Riley et al.) give a sample size from the **expected performance** and **shrinkage**; they usually ask for **more**. ::: # Topic 2 — The model {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Fit and read ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- glm(f_true, data = dev, family = binomial) round(exp(coef(m1)), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) age sexMale bmi waist fam_history 0.000 1.060 1.110 0.967 1.056 3.101 hypertension activity smoker 1.965 0.887 1.855 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Family history OR **3.1**, hypertension **2.0**, smoking **1.9**, age **1.06 per year**, waist **1.06 per cm** - The **BMI OR is 0.97**: waist and BMI carry **the same information**, so single coefficients are **unstable**. For **prediction** this is acceptable; for **explanation** it would not be ::: ## Predicted risks ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dev$risk <- predict(m1, type = "response") summary(dev$risk) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 0.002 0.035 0.077 0.120 0.156 0.864 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} new <- data.frame(age = 55, sex = factor("Male", levels = levels(dev$sex)), bmi = 29, waist = 100, fam_history = 1, hypertension = 1, activity = 2, smoker = 0) predict(m1, newdata = new, type = "response") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 0.5436867 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Risks range from **0.2% to 86%** (median 7.7%); their mean equals the **prevalence (12%)**. A 55-year-old man with BMI 29, waist 100 cm, family history, hypertension, 2 hours of activity, non-smoker has a predicted risk of **54%**. Clinicians use **risks**, not odds ratios. ::: ## Risk groups ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dev |> mutate(group = cut(risk, c(0, 0.05, 0.15, 1), labels = c("low (<5%)", "medium (5-15%)", "high (15%+)"), include.lowest = TRUE)) |> group_by(group) |> summarise(n = n(), observed = round(mean(diabetes), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 group n observed 1 low (<5%) 249 0.02 2 medium (5-15%) 266 0.102 3 high (15%+) 185 0.281 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Observed diabetes: **2%, 10%, 28%**. These look great, but they are in the **same data used to build the model**: **optimistic**. Sessions 2 to 5 show how to **measure** performance **honestly**. ::: ## The steps (TRIPOD) ::: {.good} 1. **Define** the outcome, predictors and the intended **use** (who, when, why) 2. Check the **sample size** and handle **missing data** (A7) 3. **Fit** the model; avoid unnecessary selection 4. **Evaluate**: discrimination, calibration, usefulness (Session 2) 5. **Internal validation** with optimism correction (Session 3), **shrinkage** (Session 4) 6. **External validation** and recalibration (Session 5) 7. **Report** with TRIPOD: full equation, performance, limitations ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `prediction-workshop/labs/lab1_build.R` - events, prevalence, events per variable - fit the model, predicted risks, a new patient - risk groups and the difference between cohorts ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dtkeo3.22n6nl" data-show="VGhlIG51bWJlciBvZiBldmVudHMsIHRoZSBsZXNzIGNvbW1vbiBvZiB0aGUgdHdvIG91dGNv bWVz" data-explain="VGhlIGluZm9ybWF0aW9uIGZvciBhIGJpbmFyeSBvdXRjb21lIHNpdHMgaW4gdGhlIHJhcmVy IG91dGNvbWUuIEV2ZW50cyBwZXIgdmFyaWFibGUgaXMgdGhlIHVzdWFsIHdheSB0byBqdWRn ZSBob3cgbWFueSBwYXJhbWV0ZXJzIGNhbiBiZSBlc3RpbWF0ZWQgcmVsaWFibHku"} The model has 84 events and 8 parameters. What mostly limits how many predictors you can use? - The number of events, the less common of the two outcomes - The number of adults in the cohort, whatever the outcome frequency - The number of adults without the disease, since they are the majority - The number of variables that are significant in a univariate analysis ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dtkrwu.22nl50" data-show="SXQgZ2l2ZXMgdGhlIGNoYW5jZSBmb3IgdGhpcyBwYXRpZW50LCBvbiBhIHNjYWxlIG9uZSBj YW4gYWN0IG9u" data-explain="QSByaXNrIG9mIDU0JSBjYW4gYmUgY29tcGFyZWQgd2l0aCBhIHRyZWF0bWVudCB0aHJlc2hv bGQuIEFuIG9kZHMgcmF0aW8gZGVzY3JpYmVzIHJlbGF0aXZlIGRpZmZlcmVuY2VzIGJldHdl ZW4gZ3JvdXBzLCBub3QgdGhlIGFic29sdXRlIGNoYW5jZSBmb3IgYSBwYXRpZW50Lg=="} Why is a predicted risk more useful to a clinician than an odds ratio? - It does not depend on the data that were used to develop the model - It has a narrower confidence interval than the odds ratio from the model - It gives the chance for this patient, on a scale one can act on - It can be compared directly with the odds ratios of other published models ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dtl55i.22nzmc" data-show="UHJlZGljdGlvbiBhaW1zIGF0IGFjY3VyYXRlIHJpc2tzLCBleHBsYW5hdGlvbiBhdCBhbiB1 bmJpYXNlZCBlZmZlY3Q=" data-explain="QSBwcmVkaWN0aW9uIG1vZGVsIGlzIGp1ZGdlZCBieSB0aGUgYWNjdXJhY3kgb2YgaXRzIHJp c2tzIGluIG5ldyBwYXRpZW50cywgd2hpbGUgYW4gZXhwbGFuYXRvcnkgYW5hbHlzaXMgaXMg Y29uY2VybmVkIHdpdGggdGhlIGVmZmVjdCBvZiBvbmUgZXhwb3N1cmUsIGZyZWUgb2YgY29u Zm91bmRpbmcu"} What is the difference between a prediction model and an explanatory model? - Prediction needs a randomised design, while explanation does not need one - Prediction aims at accurate risks, explanation at an unbiased effect - Prediction models must contain only variables with a causal effect on the outcome - Explanation models are judged by their AUC, prediction models by p-values ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dtlie8.22oe3q" data-show="Q29lZmZpY2llbnRzIG9mIGNvcnJlbGF0ZWQgcHJlZGljdG9ycyBhcmUgdW5zdGFibGUsIHll dCBwcmVkaWN0aW9ucyBjYW4gYmUgZ29vZA==" data-explain="V2Fpc3QgYW5kIEJNSSBjYXJyeSBhbG1vc3QgdGhlIHNhbWUgaW5mb3JtYXRpb24sIHNvIHRo ZSBzcGxpdCBvZiB0aGUgZWZmZWN0IGJldHdlZW4gdGhlbSBpcyBhcmJpdHJhcnkuIFRoZSBq b2ludCBwcmVkaWN0aW9uIGlzIG5vdCBhZmZlY3RlZCwgYnV0IHRoZSBjb2VmZmljaWVudHMg c2hvdWxkIG5vdCBiZSBpbnRlcnByZXRlZC4="} The BMI odds ratio is 0.97, although BMI is a risk factor, because waist is also in the model. What does this mean for a prediction model? - The model is invalid, so BMI should be removed from it before any prediction is made - BMI protects against diabetes once waist circumference is taken into account - Coefficients of correlated predictors are unstable, yet predictions can be good - The correlation shows that waist causes diabetes and that BMI does not ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="p1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dtlvmy.22osl4" data-show="VGhlIG1vZGVsIHdhcyBmaXR0ZWQgdG8gdGhvc2UgZGF0YSwgc28gaXQgcGFydGx5IGZpdHMg dGhlaXIgcmFuZG9tIG5vaXNl" data-explain="UGFyYW1ldGVycyBhcmUgY2hvc2VuIHRvIGZpdCB0aGUgZGV2ZWxvcG1lbnQgZGF0YSBhcyBj bG9zZWx5IGFzIHBvc3NpYmxlLCBpbmNsdWRpbmcgY2hhbmNlIHBhdHRlcm5zIHRoYXQgd2ls bCBub3QgcmVwZWF0IGluIG5ldyBwYXRpZW50cy4="} Why is the performance of a model in the data used to build it too optimistic? - Development data are collected with more accurate measurements - The predicted risks in the development data are not compared with the observed outcomes - The outcome is known for the development data, but not for new patients - The model was fitted to those data, so it partly fits their random noise ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Prediction** = accurate risks for new patients; **explanation** = unbiased effect - **Events** (not adults) limit the model: about 10 per parameter or more - Report **predicted risks** and risk groups - Single coefficients of **correlated predictors** are unstable - Performance in the **development data** is optimistic ::: **Next:** Session 2: discrimination and calibration

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
